result:
A component re-renders whenever its own state changes, its parent renders, or a context it reads changes, so unexpected renders almost always trace to one of the causes below. The React DevTools Profiler, with "Record why each component rendered" turned on, will tell you which.

The most common cause is a parent re-rendering, which re-renders every child by default regardless of props. Fix it by wrapping the child in `React.memo`, or better, by moving the changing state down into the component that actually uses it, or passing the expensive subtree as `children` so it keeps the same element identity.

The second is `memo` being defeated by props that are new on every render: inline objects, arrays and functions like `style={{...}}` or `onClick={() => ...}`. Stabilize them with `useMemo` and `useCallback`, or hoist constants out of the component.

The third is context: every consumer re-renders when the provider's `value` changes identity, and `value={{ user, setUser }}` changes on every provider render. Memoize the value, and split contexts that mix rarely and frequently changing data, or use a store with selectors.

The fourth is store selectors that return a fresh object each time, such as `useSelector(s => ({ a: s.a, b: s.b }))`. Select primitives separately or pass `shallowEqual`.

The fifth is an effect that sets state and has an unstable dependency, causing a render-effect-render loop. Fix the dependency, or compute the value during render instead of storing derived state.

The sixth is remounting rather than re-rendering, caused by unstable keys like `key={Math.random()}` or a component defined inside another component's body. Use stable ids for keys and hoist component definitions to module scope.

Finally, double renders in development only are `StrictMode` doing so deliberately, and need no fix.

If you are on React 19 with the React Compiler enabled, it handles the memoization in the second cause, and most of the first, automatically. A re-render is also only worth fixing if the Profiler shows it is actually slow.
